This paper introduces a novel approach to feature extraction, known as the Unified Structure for Feature Extraction (UNIFEED), which employs a comparative learning framework. 
The proposed structure is designed to be versatile and can be applied to various tasks, including classification, regression, and ranking. 
UNIFEED utilizes a set of auxiliary tasks, each with its own output layer, and an auxiliary loss function is used to evaluate the performance of each task. 
The structure is optimized by minimizing the average loss across all tasks, allowing for a unified and balanced approach to feature extraction. 
Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed structure, showing significant improvements in performance compared to traditional methods, particularly in low-data scenarios.
A new infinite series of star normal quotient diagrams have been identified for a specific class of groups known as twisted wreath products, extending a recent discovery by Breuer and the author.

Working with nominal data in regression models is a common task in statistics,
especially when dealing with high-dimensional datasets.  In this context, models
with a Group Lasso penalty are particularly useful for handling data sparsity
and selecting variables.  This paper introduces an enhanced version of the
Group Lasso model, specifically designed for nominal data, and establishes its
theoretical properties.  We also demonstrate the model's effectiveness through
numerical experiments and real-world applications.

We present a novel framework called ABILITY, which enhances the knowledge
structure of large language models (LLMs) through a two-phase process.
In the first phase, we employ a graph-based method to integrate structured
knowledge from multiple knowledge bases into LLMs' knowledge structures.
In the second phase, we leverage the integrated knowledge to enhance
the LLMs' performance on various downstream tasks.
Our approach is designed to be modular and adaptable, allowing for
easy incorporation of new knowledge sources and adaptation to different
tasks.
Our experiments demonstrate that the enhanced LLMs achieve significant
improvements in both knowledge reasoning and generalization capabilities.
Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ChenZhihao/ABILITY.

This study proposes a nonlocal dispersion model that can be mathematically described by a balance equation, where the flux is determined by a nonlocal function of the state. We demonstrate that this model has an exact solution and can be approximated using a local model. Notably, the relationship between the nonlocal and local models can be expressed through a specific scaling law. When analyzing the long-term behavior, we find that the nonlocal model's solution converges to a Mittag-Leffler distribution, whereas the local model's solution follows an exponential distribution. These results provide a basis for understanding the connection between nonlocal and local models and the implications of using nonlocal dispersion models.

This study focuses on panoramic image stitching, a common task in computer vision. Unlike other approaches, we consider the camera to be operating under the assumption of Euclidean geometry. We develop a method to stitch images by minimizing the number of changes required, given this assumption. We also explore the concept of "minimal solutions" in relation to Descriptive Inverse Problems and provide a theoretical basis for our approach. We then present an efficient algorithm to solve this problem and demonstrate its effectiveness through experiments.
This paper delves into the cancellation of poles in Eisenstein series for $GL(n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$, with a focus on its underlying discrete mathematics.

Parkinson's disease is a chronic neurodegenerative disorder that primarily affects the basal ganglia, resulting in motor and non-motor symptoms.
The disease's progression is marked by the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, leading to motor dysfunction.
Non-motor symptoms, which can precede motor symptoms by years, are also influenced by the accumulation of Lewy bodies in the cortex and limbic system.
Current treatments, which involve dopamine replacement therapy, are effective in managing motor symptoms but have limited impact on non-motor symptoms.
This study proposes a novel computational model that simulates the pathophysiology of Parkinson's disease in marmoset primates, which are an ideal model for studying the disease's progression.
The model is based on a biophysical framework that incorporates the brain's structural and functional connectivity, as well as the dynamics of dopamine and other neurotransmitters.
By integrating this framework with data from marmoset primates, the model is able to accurately predict the development of motor and non-motor symptoms, as well as the response to various treatment options.
This study demonstrates the potential of data-informed biophysical models to provide a comprehensive understanding of complex neurological disorders, and to inform the development of more effective treatment strategies.

When rendering line junctions on vector maps, anti-aliasing techniques can introduce unwanted artifacts due to the mismatch between the number of pixels and lines. This issue becomes more pronounced as map lines get thinner. To address this problem, we propose a novel anti-aliasing method that combines pixel-based and grid-based rendering. Our approach uses a hybrid pixel grid to calculate fill areas and then renders lines on this grid, which is scaled according to the map's line thickness. As a result, our method produces visually pleasing effects without noticeable artifacts, even for lines with varying thicknesses.

We have conducted observations of nine ultra/luminous infrared galaxies using the KOOLS-IFU on the Seimei Telescope, with redshifts below 0.04. These observations were carried out in the optical wavelength range of 0.36 to 0.92 micrometers, with a spatial resolution of 0.3 to 0.4 arcseconds and a spectral resolution of 1000 to 2000. The observations were conducted in 12 spectral orders, with a wavelength step of 0.1 to 0.2 Angstroms, and a spatial step of 0.3 to 0.4 arcseconds. The observations were conducted on the following galaxies: NGC 6090A, NGC 6240, NGC 4945, NGC 3516, NGC 3256, NGC 2992, NGC 2788, NGC 2625A, and NGC 253. The multivariate interpolation problem is addressed by a new, transcendental interpolation operator that utilizes a specific, positive definite radial basis function. This function, denoted as $\exp(-1/\|x-c\|^2)$, is based on a novel transcendental RBF. The theorem proving the positive definiteness of this function in multiple dimensions is also presented. The positive definiteness of this transcendental RBF enables the derivation of an identity that facilitates the preservation of polynomial behavior in the interpolation process. The resulting interpolation method is shown to be convergent and its convergence rate is analyzed. Theoretical findings are supported by numerical experiments.

This research focuses on developing an effective weather classification system to provide accurate forecasts and enhance public safety.  To address the lack of publicly available datasets for this purpose, a new multi-class weather dataset has been created, consisting of 10 distinct weather conditions.  To overcome the limitations of small and imbalanced datasets, a data augmentation technique using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) has been employed, resulting in a balanced dataset of 100,000 images.  To evaluate the performance of various Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architectures, a comprehensive study has been conducted, with the results showing that a ResNet-50 model achieves the highest accuracy of 99.99% when combined with the GAN-augmented dataset.  The source code and the new weather dataset are made publicly available to facilitate further research in this area.

This study introduces a novel end-to-end speech enhancement model, the Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN), which is designed to tackle the challenge of speech enhancement in a single-channel scenario.  The network's dual-path architecture, which combines a front-end feature extraction module and a back-end speech reconstruction module, enables it to effectively process speech signals.  The front-end feature extraction module utilizes a multi-scale convolutional layer to capture both local and global contextual information, while the back-end speech reconstruction module utilizes a multi-layer bidirectional recurrent neural network to generate a high-quality output.  The DPCRN model is trained using a mean squared error loss function and is evaluated on the AMI meeting corpus and the AMI single-talker corpus.  The results show that the DPCRN model outperforms several state-of-the-art speech enhancement models, including Conv-TasNet, FSE-Net, and SE-Net, in terms of objective quality metrics such as PESQ and PMOS.  The DPCRN model is also shown to be particularly effective in terms of computational efficiency, requiring fewer computational resources than several other speech enhancement models.

The expansion rate of the universe is influenced by $f(R)$ gravity, which can be modified from standard general relativity. This study investigates how such modifications, combined with the effects of heavy neutrinos, impact the size of dark matter halos. We simulated the formation of dark matter halos in various $f(R)$ gravity models and mass ranges of sterile neutrinos, and found that the halo sizes are significantly affected by both factors. The results indicate that the halo sizes can be used to constrain the parameters of $f(R)$ gravity and heavy neutrinos, and that the effects of both factors can be distinguished by analyzing halo sizes at different redshifts.

The simulation is based on a two-fluid version of the Anelastic Convection and Radiative Transfer model, which is then compared to single-fluid simulations. The results show that the two-fluid simulations accurately represent convection, with the two fluids experiencing similar temperatures and velocities. The simulation is also used to examine the effects of varying mass ratios and eddy diffusivities on convection, with the findings indicating that the two fluids behave similarly when diffusivities are high, but start to diverge when diffusivities are low. The study also reveals that the two fluids can exhibit different behaviors when subjected to different mass ratios, with the heavier fluid being more affected by the mass ratio than the lighter fluid. This research proposes a novel method to generate genuine multipartite entanglement among initially uncorrelated particles by exploiting the Jaynes-Cummings interactions. By applying a sequence of local interactions between each particle and its associated cavity, we demonstrate the ability to create various forms of multipartite entanglement, including $N$-qubit W-state and GHZ-type entanglement. Furthermore, we show that our method can also produce other types of entangled states, such as generalized W-state, generalized GHZ-state, and other M-qubit states with arbitrary amplitudes.

The CMS Phase-1 Pixel Pilot Layer is a limited sensor area, covering 10% of the Phase-1 Pixel Detector, which is used to test and validate the performance of the new pixel technology. This paper examines the reconstruction of particles hitting the outer layer of the Pixel Pilot, analyzing how well the system can track and measure the trajectories of charged particles. The results show that the system can accurately reconstruct the tracks of particles with a high level of precision, with a small level of bias in the track measurements. The system can also accurately measure the momentum of particles with a level of precision that is consistent with the expected level of precision based on the level of noise in the system. The results are compared to the performance of the older Phase-2 and Phase-1 Pixel Detectors, and the system is shown to have a level of performance that is similar to the older detectors. The paper also discusses the impact of the system on the reconstruction of jets and the detection of photons, and the system is shown to have a level of performance that is consistent with the expected level of performance based on the level of noise in the system.

Using a non-perturbative approach, specifically the combined lattice and continuum Lattice Effective Field Theory, we have derived a Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral function for the SU(2) scalar glueball in the gluon condensate channel. Our findings indicate a discrete pole at approximately 2.9 GeV, which we attribute to be the glueball mass, and a spectral continuum starting from around 3.5 GeV.

Social media platforms have gained immense popularity, with Twitter being a prime example.  Monitoring public opinion on Twitter has become an essential tool for gauging sentiment towards various topics, events, and individuals.  This study introduces a novel approach to classifying Twitter posts based on sentiment, utilizing Long Short-Term Memory networks.  Our method involves extracting relevant keywords from tweets, incorporating them into the input data, and leveraging pre-trained word embeddings.  Our proposed technique was tested on three well-known datasets, with results showing a significant improvement in accuracy compared to existing methods.  Our model achieved an accuracy of 84.1% on the SemEval-2013 Task 4 dataset, 81.1% on the Twitter-UAM-15 dataset, and 79.1% on the Twitter-16 dataset.

We have analyzed the thermodynamic properties of a non-linear charged AdS black hole, characterized by a Maxwell's scalar field, and found that a shadow phase transition occurs when the spacetime's charge surpasses a critical value. This effect can be understood through the Ruppeimer and Overkumer metrics, which exhibit a conical singularity at the point of transition. Interestingly, this threshold corresponds to the point where the outer horizon of the black hole vanishes, indicating a shift from a non-extremal to an extremal state.

This study aims to provide a general framework for analyzing changes in a quantum system's entanglement and the onset of two subsystems' correlation, using the 3D tomographic representation. By applying this framework to a specific scenario, we investigate the entanglement and subsequent correlation between two parts of a quantum system, known as the EPR-Bohm setup.

Conversational agents that can adapt to various scenarios and maintain a specific persona are crucial for developing advanced systems. These systems can be utilized in diverse applications, such as creating engaging chatbots, lifelike virtual characters in video games, and sophisticated conversational interfaces. In this study, we introduce a novel open-domain conversation framework that enables a single model to effectively embody a specific role and engage in natural, context-aware dialogues. Our approach involves a single, unified model that leverages a large language model and additional components to ensure the conversation adheres to the defined role. Utilizing a large-scale dataset comprising over 1.5 million dialogues and featuring a diverse range of roles, we evaluate our framework and demonstrate its effectiveness in maintaining the defined role, generating high-quality responses, and following the flow of the conversation. Our results indicate that our proposed method outperforms existing baselines in these tasks. Furthermore, we make our dataset and framework publicly available to facilitate further research in this area.

This study employs a robust pest control strategy to tackle the challenge of strawberry disease prevention. By utilizing a sophisticated reward function, we can effectively address the inherent limitations of traditional methods. Our approach is tested on a Strawberry dataset, and our results demonstrate significant improvements in control accuracy and efficiency compared to existing techniques.

360-degree videos are an emerging technology that enables users to have an immersive experience in various locations. To enhance this experience, it is crucial to develop a system that can accurately predict the user's viewpoint at the end of the video. This prediction is essential for creating a seamless transition when moving to the next scene. In this study, we introduce a novel task of viewport forecasting, which aims to predict the user's viewpoint at the end of the video. We also propose a baseline model that utilizes caption information to effectively predict the user's viewpoint. Our approach outperforms existing methods that rely solely on visual information, demonstrating the effectiveness of incorporating caption information. We make our dataset and code publicly available to facilitate future research in this area.

Tensor network methods have been widely used to model complex quantum systems, particularly in scenarios where exact solutions are unattainable. However, a significant limitation of these methods is their lack of a clear physical interpretation, which hinders their ability to accurately represent thermal states and time-dependent systems. In response to this challenge, we introduce a novel tensor network framework that incorporates local precision variations to better capture the properties of thermal states and systems undergoing temporal evolution. By employing a precise matrix product operator representation, we demonstrate that our framework can accurately model the behavior of these systems while providing a more intuitive understanding of their underlying quantum dynamics. Furthermore, we show that our approach can be applied to a range of physical scenarios, including the study of thermal phase transitions and the Kondo effect, and offers a powerful tool for exploring the broader field of many-body physics.

This study proposes a decoupling approach for limited and ambiguous information, such as indirect observations, by separating it into independent components. A novel method called the decoupling approximation technique is introduced, which involves modeling restricted effectiveness as a combination of independent, unrelated variables. A scale-oriented criterion is used to identify the optimal combination, allowing for the approximation of complex, uncertain situations. This method is particularly useful in situations where there is limited information and multiple possible explanations for an observed phenomenon. The decoupling approach is demonstrated through a case study involving the identification of a lost hiker, where it is used to interpret conflicting GPS data and other indirect observations.

This study introduces a novel definition of nonisotropic $p$-capacity in R^n, derives an inequality linking nonisotropic Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator and capacity, and establishes an inequality akin to nonisotropic Poincare inequality. It also defines isotropic and nonisotropic mixed Monge-Ampere measure and derives an inequality akin to mixed Monge-Ampere measure Minkowski inequality.

The MICROSCOPE satellite is set to significantly enhance our understanding of the weak equivalence principle (WEP) by precisely measuring the acceleration of two test masses made of different materials in space. The test mass accelerations are expected to be influenced by various forces, including electrostatic and magnetic forces, which can be accurately controlled and minimized. However, an uncontrolled force known as a glitch can occur due to sudden changes in the test mass's temperature, leading to a temporary imbalance in the mass distribution. This study aims to analyze the impact of glitches on the MICROSCOPE test of the WEP, taking into account the measurement uncertainties and the distribution of the test mass's acceleration. The study finds that the impact of glitches on the expected outcome of the test is minimal, with a 90% confidence interval of -1.1 x 10^-14 to 1.1 x 10^-14, which is significantly smaller than the total error margin of the test. The study also predicts that the impact of glitches on the expected outcome of the test will be even smaller in the future, with a 90% confidence interval of -0.04 x 10^-14 to 0.04 x 10^-14. We investigate a system of non-interacting, self-propelled colloidal particles that are subjected to an activity gradient. The particles experience different activity levels and are driven to move from regions of high activity to regions of low activity. This setup is analogous to the well-known Soret effect, where particles move in response to a temperature gradient. We develop a theoretical model to describe the dynamics of the particles and find that the system can be characterized by a dimensionless activity number. This activity number determines the behavior of the particles and can lead to the formation of distinct regions of high and low activity. We also find that the particles can exhibit a variety of different patterns of motion, including the formation of stable clusters and oscillatory behavior. These findings have implications for the design of active matter systems and could lead to new ways of controlling the motion of particles in response to activity gradients.

The k-strong shortest route union cover problem involves selecting the minimum number of k-strong shortest path covers to completely cover a graph G, denoted as $\chi_{k-SSRC}(G)$. In this study, we establish that $\chi_{k-SSRC}(G)$ is NP-hard for G being a planar graph with a maximum degree of four, and we develop a 4-approximation algorithm for $\chi_{k-SSRC}(Q_n)$, where $Q_n$ is a hypercube graph, and a 3-approximation algorithm for $\chi_{k-SSRC}(C_m \otimes C_n)$, where $C_m \otimes C_n$ is a torus graph.

The color dipole gluon PDF, which is non-zero only at the highest order in small-x, is shown to be affected by infrared renormalons, with its Borel transform exhibiting poles in the interval [0,1]. This is attributed to the presence of both even and odd powers of $\ln(x)$ in the color dipole gluon PDF, with the latter being a result of the impact of the odd-bugle gluon PDF. As a result, the color dipole gluon PDF is expected to exhibit an unresumable ambiguity at the perturbative level, which is in contrast to the positive gluon PDF that is expected to be free of such renormalon effects.

We analyze a frog model on a binary tree, where an infinite number of frogs are initially located at the root, with one active frog and the rest dormant. When an active frog visits a vertex, it leaves a new frog there and may become inactive with a certain probability. We find the essential density, which is the minimum density required for the system to eventually occupy all vertices of the tree.

Two-dimensional materials have gained significant attention due to their unique electronic and optical properties, which can be harnessed for various applications. In this study, we present a novel approach to engineering photonic lattices on top insulating two-dimensional van der Waals crystals, which allows for precise control over light propagation. By utilizing a photo-induced lattice with asymmetric unit cells, we demonstrate the ability to create stable, one-way photonic states that are robust against disorder. Our research reveals that the topological properties of these states can be tuned through changes in lattice orientation, which has implications for the development of compact and efficient photonic devices. Our findings provide a foundation for the development of new photonic devices based on two-dimensional van der Waals crystals, which could have applications in areas such as quantum information processing and photonic integrated circuits.

This paper introduces a novel approach to transfer learning, which utilizes a decision-based black-box framework to train models on tasks they have not been explicitly designed for. By leveraging the vast amount of knowledge contained in such a framework, our method enables zero-shot transfer learning without the need for access to the underlying data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through multiple experiments, including a task where we transfer a trained model from a black-box framework to a fully supervised learning task, achieving comparable performance to a model trained from scratch. We also explore the potential of our method to transfer a model to a different task, such as a sentiment analysis task, and show that our approach can achieve competitive performance with a small amount of labeled data.

Researchers have analyzed data from the LHCb experiment at the LHC, specifically looking at $B^0_s$ decaying into $\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ and $\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L$ final states. By studying 3.0 inverse femtobarns of data collected at 7 TeV, scientists have determined the branching fractions for these decays to be $1.4 \times 10^{-4}$ and $0.6 \times 10^{-4}$ respectively, with a statistical significance of 3.2 standard deviations.

We present an efficient method to construct the lattice of submodules for a specific type of module, specifically those with a single layer of composition components, using a subset of the module's composition structure and a subset of its submodule lattice. Our proposed lattice construction method is proven to be lattice-isomorphic to the actual lattice of submodules.

A Strong Geodetic set for a graph G is defined as a subset S of its vertices, where every vertex outside of S lies on a unique shortest path between two vertices in S. The minimum Strong Geodetic set problem seeks to find the smallest possible subset that meets this criterion. This paper investigates the computational complexity of this problem, which has been previously studied but not extensively in the context of parameterized algorithms. It has been proven that the Strong Geodetic set problem is NP-complete for various graph types, including bipartite, planar, and split graphs. Additionally, it has been shown that the problem is W[1]-hard to parameterize by solution size, and inapproximable within a factor of 1.000001 under the Unique Games Conjecture. The paper also explores the approximability of the problem under the assumption of the Unique Games Conjecture, showing that it can be approximated within a factor of 1.5, and under the assumption of ETH, it can be approximated within a factor of 1.3606.

The primary objective of the mimicry learning problem is to develop an efficient algorithm that can be mimicked by an optimal solution, even when given access to a subpar solution. This research focuses on a specific scenario where the mimicked solution has a significantly higher quality than the available sample. We examine the problem within the context of learning linear concepts using noisy comparisons, a common application in recommendation systems. We first establish a lower bound of $\Omega(d^2/\epsilon^2)$ for this setting, and then propose an efficient algorithm that achieves this bound when the available sample is at least $10\cdot (d^2/\epsilon^2)$ times worse than the desired factor. We also explore a more general setting where the available sample is $s$ times worse than the desired factor, and show that our near-optimal bound of $O(d^2/\epsilon^2 + \sqrt{sd})$ holds, and that this is supported by a corresponding lower bound of $\Omega(d^2/\epsilon^2 + \sqrt{sd})$.

In cooperative settings, a learner can learn more effectively by observing both successful and unsuccessful actions of an expert, yet most existing approaches only utilize examples of successful actions. This paper introduces a novel framework for learning from a cooperative expert through implicit feedback, where the expert provides a score for the learner's action based on their current state and action history. We present a new algorithm that learns from this type of feedback, and demonstrate its efficiency through experiments, showing significant improvements in performance compared to baseline methods.

This study introduces a new approach to calculating absolute metric values in coding theory, specifically for Generalized Algebraic Codes (GACs) with rectangular algebraic structures. The proposed calculation method is versatile and can be applied to various types of GACs, including Binary Algebraic Codes (BACs), Quaternary Algebraic Codes (GACs) with binary rectangular algebraic structures, and Gaussian Algebraic Codes (GACs) with quaternary algebraic structures. The study demonstrates the proposed calculation method's effectiveness by applying it to a specific GAC with a binary rectangular algebraic structure and quaternary algebraic properties.

This paper proposes a novel approach to enhance neural machine translation by incorporating action space reinforcement learning. Unlike previous methods that focus on improving word selection, our approach considers sentence-level action space and leverages reinforcement learning to optimize the entire hypothesis generation process. We introduce a universal action space that combines word selection and reordering, allowing the model to generate high-quality translations more efficiently. Experimental results on the IWSLT 2017 English-to-German dataset demonstrate significant improvements in translation accuracy and human evaluation, outperforming strong baseline models.

This research paper presents an innovative robot calibration method that utilizes unlmarked images and a learning-based approach to estimate the robot's end-effector position. By leveraging a robot-depth camera, we develop a method to adjust the camera's adjustment parameters and predict the end-effector's location in 3D space. Our approach involves training a neural network to adjust the camera parameters and a separate network to estimate the end-effector position. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through experiments with a robot, showing that it can accurately adjust the camera parameters and estimate the end-effector position.

This study focuses on a specific region within a quantum entanglement transition, known as the quantum critical entanglement phase transition (QFS). We first define and characterize the QFS region, then explore its properties through various methods, including numerical simulations and theoretical analysis. We find that the QFS region is defined by a balance between disorder and interactions, and that its shape and size are influenced by the system's dimension and geometry. We also propose a new quantity, the QFS area velocity, which provides insight into the nature of the quantum critical point and its relationship to other types of critical behavior.

The rise of partisan online news platforms has led to increased political polarization, particularly in the United States. Studies have shown that consuming news from sources aligned with one's own political views reinforces existing biases. This study leverages social media data to examine the political leanings of Twitter users who consume news from Facebook pages, using a large-scale dataset of over 1.5 million users and their associated political profiles. By applying supervised learning techniques, we classify users as either liberal, conservative, or moderate based on their Facebook posts. Our analysis reveals a significant correlation between the political orientation of the news sources consumed and the political leanings of the consumers themselves. Users who consume news from highly partisan sources tend to have more extreme political views compared to those who consume from less polarized sources. This study provides valuable insights into the growing issue of political division in online news consumption.

We examine the word problem in the R. Thompson group V, which can be broken down into three distinct categories: words that represent the identity, those that are not, and the identities found within subgroups of V. A particular subgroup of V, denoted as F, is isomorphic to the free group of rank 2. We demonstrate that the set of identities within F constitutes a non-contextual but semi-algebraic language. Furthermore, we explore a particular subgroup of V, denoted as W, which is isomorphic to the direct product of two free groups of rank 2, and show that the set of identities within W is not semi-algebraic.

We present an experimental setup that creates a non-equilibrium steady state in a quantum system, achieved by periodically driving a two-level system. Our setup, using an electron spin in a GaAs quantum dot, allows us to observe a distinct response pattern that can be explained by a simple theoretical model. We find that the system's behavior is determined by the competition between the driving force and the system's internal energy levels, leading to a clear separation between the two components of the response pattern.
We examine how various linear operators, applied in sequence, contribute to biharmonic hypersurfaces within the Euclidean space.

Given positive integers $p$ and $q$ that share no common factors, a set $S$ is considered $p/q$-identifiable when the set of remainders produced by dividing its elements by $q$ can be uniquely determined from the corresponding remainders when divided by $p$. This paper aims to provide a straightforward method for calculating $p/q$-identifiable sets, along with specific examples and data for sets defined by polynomials with integer coefficients.

This model is designed to address the axion decay mode problem, where the decay of an unstable axion into photons can create a background of noise in the experiments that are searching for axions. The LAMOST time-domain exploration project is set to significantly enhance our understanding of stellar variability and stellar activity, as well as the evolution of stars and the detection of exoplanets. This project will involve the use of four dedicated $K$2 plates, which will be used to observe a vast range of stars across different stages of development. In this paper, we present preliminary findings based on the initial data from the LAMOST time-domain exploration project. We analyzed the light curves of over 100,000 stars and identified various patterns of variability, including the characteristics of variable stars, the frequency of binary systems, and the presence of exoplanets. We also explored the relationship between stellar activity and the occurrence of binary systems, as well as the impact of exoplanets on the behavior of their host stars. These preliminary results demonstrate the potential of the LAMOST time-domain exploration project to provide valuable insights into the nature of stars and their interactions with other celestial bodies.

This study introduces an innovative 3D semantic segmentation network called Edge-Gated CNN, which uniquely separates semantic segmentation into two distinct stages: a boundary segmentation stage and a semantic segmentation stage. By initially identifying object boundaries, the edge detection stage leverages the precise spatial information to enhance the subsequent stage's performance. Furthermore, the Edge-Gated CNN employs a gated fusion module to integrate the high-level semantic information from the first stage with the spatial information from the second stage, leading to improved semantic segmentation outcomes. Experimental results on the MSK-Cancer dataset demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method over existing approaches, achieving a Dice score of 0.8111 in prostate segmentation and 0.8200 in lymph node segmentation.

MongoDB is a popular NoSQL database that offers high performance and scalability, but lacks the ability to handle complex queries and transactions efficiently. To address this limitation, we developed a transactional integrity validator for MongoDB that can be used to ensure data consistency and accuracy. Our validator is designed to work with existing MongoDB applications and can be used to detect errors and anomalies in real-time. We tested our approach on various MongoDB deployments and found that it can effectively identify issues and maintain data integrity.

We demonstrate that the chromatic symmetric polynomials of trees possess $e$-positivity, an attribute first identified by Chow in 2014. This finding allows us to derive $e$-positivity for the inverse of the lower triangular matrix composed of Kostka numbers associated with partitions of $n$ into $k$ parts, a result first proved by Assaf and Tsymbaliuk in 2018. Furthermore, we provide a combinatorial interpretation for this $e$-positivity based on the charge statistic.

To tackle the issue of perception relabeling and reshuffling in a consistent manner, we introduce a new technique called Hindsight Summarization. This method leverages a pre-trained language model to generate concise descriptions of images, which are then used to train a model that learns to predict human judgments of resampled images. Our experiments show that this approach outperforms other methods, including random models and models trained using image features, on various datasets. To further enhance the interpretability of the predictions, we conduct additional experiments and create visualizations to illustrate the characteristics of images that are perceived as having high or low executive ability.

This paper introduces a novel approach to identifying implicit bias in deep learning models trained on medical image datasets. We employ demographic information from dataset metadata to pinpoint implicit bias through innate bias detection metrics. We analyzed demographic information from three medical image datasets, identifying significant disparities in race and gender distribution. We trained deep learning models on these datasets and found evidence of implicit bias in two of them. We also explored the impact of data augmentation and re-sampling techniques on bias reduction. Our findings demonstrate that data augmentation and re-sampling can mitigate implicit bias, but the issue of innate bias in medical image datasets remains unresolved.

This study delves into the hidden structural and dynamic aspects of complex networks, using spin-reversal processes in nanoscale assemblies influenced by both pairwise and triangular interactions as a case study. The assembly's structure, characterized by a pairwise interaction matrix and a triangular interaction supermatrix, comprises both concealed and visible components. The pairwise interactions, while defining the assembly's overall geometry, often contain insignificant elements that do not contribute to its stability. The study reveals that the stability of the assembly is determined by the stronger, more interconnected subgroups within the supermatrix, rather than the stronger but less interconnected pairwise interactions. The study also uncovers that the assembly's dynamics are governed by its concealed geometry, with the stronger, more interconnected subgroups within the supermatrix dominating the assembly's behavior. The study further explores the impact of an external magnetic field on the assembly, revealing that the stronger, more interconnected subgroups within the supermatrix are more resistant to spin-flipping processes, leading to a more pronounced memory effect. The study utilizes a combination of graph theory, graph coloring, and Monte Carlo simulations to analyze and visualize the assembly's structure and dynamics, providing valuable insights into the hidden aspects of complex systems.

A phenomenon known as solar breeze has been observed in the inner solar system for over a century, with the sun continuously emitting plasma and magnetic fields into space. The Parker Solar Probe, launched in 2018, has provided unprecedented measurements of solar breeze conditions near the orbit of Venus, with data collected by the WISPR and FIELDS instruments. The WISPR instrument measures the flow of solar plasma, while the FIELDS instrument measures magnetic fields and electromagnetic waves. The data from these instruments reveal that the solar breeze flows in a pattern that resembles a fluid, with the flow being influenced by the sun's magnetic field. The FIELDS data also show that the solar breeze contains electromagnetic waves that play a crucial role in accelerating particles and heating the solar breeze. The data from the WISPR and FIELDS instruments provide valuable insights into the complex interactions between the sun and the solar system, with implications for understanding space weather and its effects on Earth and other planets.

Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) is a challenging task in the field of affective computing, primarily due to the scarcity of high-quality labeled training data. In this study, we focus on Domain Adapting Deep Reinforcement Learning (DA-DRL) for SER, which is a crucial step towards developing an affective computing system capable of identifying user emotions in real-world scenarios. We propose a novel approach that combines a Domain Adaptation Network (DAN) with a Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) algorithm to achieve accurate SER. The DAN is trained to adapt the distribution of training data to that of test data, while the DDPG algorithm is used to train the DAN by providing a reward signal based on the accuracy of emotion prediction. Experimental results show that our approach outperforms existing methods, including supervised learning and other reinforcement learning algorithms, on two publicly available datasets, including the SAVEE and CREMA-D datasets.

We have conducted a study on the magnetic properties of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ under high pressure, using nuclear forward scattering at the Fe $K$ edge. Our experiments were carried out at various temperatures and pressures up to 10 GPa. Our results indicate that Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ exhibits weak magnetic ordering at 2 K, with a transition temperature of 0.1 K under ambient pressure. Under high pressure, the magnetic transition temperature increases, with a value of 0.4 K at 10 GPa. Our analysis of the magnetic structure reveals that the ordered magnetic moments are primarily located at the Fe$^{3+}$ sites, with a magnitude of 0.1 $\mu_B$ under ambient pressure and 0.2 $\mu_B$ at 10 GPa. Our findings suggest that the magnetic ordering in Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ is consistent with the RKKY interaction, and the pressure-induced changes in the magnetic transition temperature can be attributed to the changes in the RKKY interaction.

This research paper examines the uncertainty in solving the shortest route problem, 
specifically when some parameters are subject to variability. It focuses on a scenario 
where a shortest route is influenced by two types of random variables: one that changes 
discretely and another that varies continuously. The study aims to determine the 
uncertainty limits for the length of the shortest route under these conditions. It also 
applies these findings to a free flight path optimization issue, taking into account 
variable wind speeds and air traffic.

Researchers have extensively studied intense shock waves in the expanding universe, particularly those caused by massive explosions near the universe's center. This paper presents an exact solution for a spherical shock wave propagating through a universe filled with a uniform, heat-conducting fluid. The solution is derived using a specific equation of state and initial conditions that match the behavior of a fluid affected by an intense shock wave. The solution also reveals the impact of heat conduction on the structure of the shock wave and the behavior of the fluid behind the wave. The solution is also compared to the solution for a universe without heat conduction.

This study investigates the shape of the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^{+}\nu_{\mu}$ decay rate as a function of the $D_s^{*-}$ mass. Using data from 7.3 inverse femtobarns of $B$-meson decays collected by the LHCb experiment, researchers determined the decay rate by fitting the $D_s^{*-}$ mass distribution to extract $B_s^0$ decay products and then fitting the resulting rate distribution. The results indicate that a quadratic function best describes the shape of the distribution, with a chi-squared per degree of freedom of 1.01. This finding is consistent with theoretical predictions made by various models.

We establish a connection between the classical Hermite polynomials and a specific type of quantum mechanical system, the monodromy-free Schrödinger courants. This link is then used to derive the differential equation for the Hermite polynomials from the monodromy-free condition. Furthermore, we show that the monodromy-free condition is equivalent to the known quantization condition for the harmonic oscillator. This equivalence allows us to recover the properties of the Hermite polynomials, including their degree, leading coefficient, and recursion relation. Additionally, we explore the relationship between the monodromy-free Schrödinger courants and the Painlevé transcendents, specifically the second and third Painlevé transcendents. This connection is made through a transformation of the monodromy-free equation, which yields a system of differential equations that is equivalent to the second and third Painlevé transcendents.

When peeling adhesive tape from a smooth surface, a series of irregular snapping sounds occur as it unrolls. This phenomenon, which has been extensively studied, is now understood through a new theoretical framework that reveals hidden patterns within the apparent randomness. The key to this understanding lies in the fact that the tape's unrolling process is influenced by a conserved quantity, its total length, which leads to an underlying symmetry in the system. This symmetry can be utilized to analyze the process using a simplified model, which shows that the sound patterns exhibit a form of temporal clustering. This clustering behavior is a manifestation of the system's tendency to settle into a stable state, which is then disrupted by sudden changes that produce the observed sound. The framework developed in this study provides a means of quantifying this clustering and predicting the distribution of intervals between sounds, which can be tested experimentally.

We examine the impact of thermal fluctuations on the phase dynamics of planar Josephson junctions and small SQUIDs, specifically focusing on their noise characteristics. A theoretical model is developed to predict the phase's autocorrelation function, taking into account the system's temperature and the presence of external magnetic fields. Our model is validated through Monte Carlo simulations and experimental data from planar Josephson junctions and SQUIDs. The results show that the model accurately captures the phase's behavior at low temperatures, but deviates from the data at higher temperatures due to the increased influence of thermal noise. The model also reveals that the phase's dynamics are highly sensitive to the presence of external magnetic fields, with the autocorrelation function exhibiting distinct patterns in response to varying field strengths.

We've identified a novel type of non-abelian ether-like term in the effective action that arises from thermal effects in 2+1 dimensional SU(N) Yang-Mills theory. This discovery enables us to derive thermal properties of this non-abelian theory, specifically the specific heat and the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law. Additionally, we've applied this understanding to a Schwinger model, where we can calculate the temperature-dependent mass gap.

This research presents a new method for pricing options under delta hedging that takes into account transaction costs and collateral expenses. The conventional approach of static delta hedging is found to be inadequate, as it does not accurately account for the costs of selling assets to finance the hedging process. The proposed method of dynamic delta hedging is demonstrated through a model that incorporates the option's underlying asset and the risk-free interest rate. The model's results are expressed through a new pricing equation that is derived through the application of the dynamic hedging approach. The research also compares the effects of static and dynamic delta hedging on the option's price and provides insights into the behavior of the option's delta under different hedging strategies.

This research examines the effective properties of a periodic composite material with a periodic structure and differential constraints, specifically when the scale parameter approaches zero and the contrast between components is extremely high. The study focuses on a one-dimensional model with a high-contrast factor of $\varepsilon^{-2}$ and differential constraints represented by an $n$-th order Sobolev space. The research reveals that the homogenized model's effective contrast depends on the material properties and the order of the differential operator, and the results are applicable to various fields, including elasticity, fluid dynamics, and quantum mechanics.

We have analyzed tidal structures in a substantial sample of 10,000 early-type galaxies from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program, which spans a wide range of luminosities from -11.5 to -21.5 in solar units. By examining tidal tails and ears, we found that tidal features become more prevalent as luminosity decreases, with a significant increase in galaxies with tidal tails and ears in the lower luminosity range. We also discovered that tidal features are more common in massive galaxies with high stellar mass and specific star formation rates, as well as in galaxies with large effective radii and low central surface brightness. We also found that tidal features are more prevalent in galaxies with high velocity dispersions and low central mass concentrations. We also found that tidal features are more common in galaxies that are undergoing mergers, with a merger rate that is significantly higher in galaxies with tidal tails and ears compared to those without tidal features. We also found that the merger rate is consistent with previous studies, with a value of 0.004 per Gyr for galaxies with tidal tails and ears. We also found that the merger rate is consistent with the rate of major mergers predicted by the Lambda Cold Dark Matter model. We also found that tidal features are more common in galaxies that are undergoing minor mergers, with a merger rate that is significantly higher in galaxies with tidal tails and ears compared to those without tidal features. A key aspect of economic growth models is understanding how opportunities are passed down through generations. In this study, we examine a dynamic model where individuals' economic status is influenced by their own actions and the circumstances of their parents. The key feature of this model is that it allows for the possibility of changing circumstances across generations. We analyze the impact of different policies on the distribution of opportunities in this model, specifically focusing on the distribution of starting points for individuals in different generations. The results show that, under certain conditions, the distribution of opportunities can be described by a system of equations that can be solved to determine the long-term behavior of the model. The study also considers the effect of different policies on this distribution, specifically examining the impact of randomizing the distribution of opportunities. The findings have implications for understanding the transmission of advantages and disadvantages across generations and the role of government in shaping these outcomes.

This paper presents an innovative approach to reverse engineering optical systems, particularly high-power laser systems. Our method employs a combination of advanced techniques, including high-speed camera analysis, interferometry, and machine learning algorithms, to accurately reconstruct the internal components of these systems. By doing so, we can efficiently evaluate and optimize their performance, ensuring they meet the highest safety and efficiency standards.

We demonstrate that for any incompressible subset K of Lp (where p is between 1 and infinity), there exists a point q less than p such that K can be isometrically embedded into a space with a dimension one unit higher than its current dimension, but no better than this.

A novel approach to beam analysis, known as brightness scanning, is introduced.
Its principles are explained and its advantages over conventional methods are highlighted.
The scanning method's capabilities are demonstrated through simulations and experimental results.
These results indicate that beam parameters can be accurately determined through brightness scanning,
with a notable advantage being its immunity to background noise.

This paper introduces a distributed optimization algorithm that enables agents to find an optimal solution under linear communication constraints, even when some agents are compromised. The algorithm employs quantized updates to reduce communication overhead, but this can lead to solution inaccuracies. To address this issue, we propose a new method that combines quantized and distributed subgradient optimization, which can handle malicious attacks and reduce communication costs. Our algorithm is shown to converge to a neighborhood of the optimal solution, with the neighborhood size depending on the level of attack and quantization error. Numerical simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

The precise measurement of the polarization of the cosmic microwave background is crucial for studying the early universe, but it is hindered by instrumental systematic errors. These errors can be challenging to model and account for, and can significantly impact the accuracy of the data. To address this issue, we have developed a new tool called s4cmb, which allows researchers to simulate instrumental systematic errors in the measurement of the polarization of the cosmic microwave background. s4cmb is based on the popular software package simall and is designed to be user-friendly and efficient. It can simulate a wide range of instrumental systematic errors, including beam asymmetries, pixel asymmetries, and 1/f noise, and can do so for multiple experiments simultaneously. s4cmb is also optimized for high-performance computing and can run on a variety of computing platforms. We demonstrate the capabilities of s4cmb by simulating instrumental systematic errors for the Simulated Simons Observatory and Simulated CMB-Sync experiments, and show how it can be used to analyze the impact of these errors on the data. s4cmb is an essential tool for researchers working on the polarization of the cosmic microwave background, and is available for download from the s4cmb GitHub repository.

Recent advancements in pre-trained language models have achieved remarkable success in numerous NLP tasks.  However, their inner workings and underlying principles are still not fully understood.  To shed light on this topic, we focus on a specific task, the word arrangement problem, and examine the decision-making process of these models through various experiments.  Our findings reveal that pre-trained language models excel at this task due to their ability to learn the statistical relationships between words, rather than any inherent understanding of word order.  To test this hypothesis, we conduct a series of experiments, including a controlled manipulation of word order, and observe the models' performance.  Our results suggest that the models' ability to learn the distribution of words is crucial for their success in this task.  To further validate this finding, we introduce a novel intervention strategy, which involves modifying the input to the models in a way that mimics the altered word distribution.  Our results show that this intervention significantly impairs the models' performance, providing strong evidence for our proposed explanation.  Our work contributes to a deeper understanding of the inner workings of pre-trained language models and has implications for future research in this area.

Deepfake technology, a sophisticated form of media manipulation, can create highly convincing fake videos that pose a significant threat to social stability.  Deepfake detection is a complex task due to the lack of available data and the subtle artifacts that are difficult to capture.  In this paper, we introduce a novel approach called the Multi-Domain Cross Sewn Network (MD-CSDNetwork) for deepfake detection.  Our method is based on a cross-domain detection framework that utilizes a dual-branch network to extract features from both the real and generated domains.  Our approach is unique in that it is one of the few detection methods that utilizes a multi-domain approach.  Our method is designed to extract more comprehensive features by combining features from both domains.  Our network is further enhanced by a cross-domain attention module that allows the two branches to share information and focus on the most relevant features.  Our method is also trained using a novel multi-task learning approach that allows the network to learn multiple tasks simultaneously.  Our approach is evaluated on three popular deepfake datasets, and the results show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and robustness.  Our method is also shown to be effective in detecting deepfakes that are created using a variety of techniques and algorithms.

To enhance the decoding speed of LDPC codes, a new optimization criterion is proposed, which involves minimizing a specific metric based on the degree-degree graph of the code. This criterion is then applied to the design of LDPC codes, resulting in a set of optimized check node degree distributions that maximize decoding performance.

A critical component of practical quantum key distribution (QKD) systems is the decoy-state method, which relies on the randomization of quantum phase to thwart photon number splitting attacks. In this research, we introduce a novel attack that bypasses the safety of phase randomization by exploiting an overlooked vulnerability in how quantum phase is handled within the system. Our attack targets a common setup where the attacker intercepts and replaces the signal and decoy photons with new ones that have randomly assigned phases. We demonstrate that this attack can be successfully executed even when the quantum phase is randomly selected, and we explore the impact of the attack on the key rate and security of the system. Our findings suggest that the attack can be mitigated by employing more sophisticated source characterization techniques or by using alternative methods to ensure the security of the quantum channel.

This paper outlines the central network management procedures that are essential for the efficient operation of next-generation cellular networks.
We examine the critical functions of these processes, which are designed to automate the configuration and optimization of network parameters, thereby ensuring optimal performance and cost-effectiveness.
In particular, we discuss the challenges associated with the dynamic adjustment of network capacity in response to fluctuating traffic patterns and the deployment of network infrastructure to minimize operational costs.
We also explore the potential benefits of these processes, which include improved user experience, reduced network congestion, and enhanced energy efficiency.

In 1923, R. Menger introduced a generalization of metric spaces, known as convex metric spaces, to extend the concept of Minkowski spaces. He then investigated the properties of angle spaces, extending the work of Finsler and others. Building on Menger's work, we introduce a new axiom for angle spaces and establish a theorem that implies a specific equality for angles. This new axiom is then used to establish theorems that confirm long-standing conjectures by Menger regarding the non-triviality of angle spaces and their isometric equivalence to a specific type of space.

This paper investigates the successive minima of various orderings of algebraic integers within a specific number field K, specifically focusing on finding upper and lower bounds for these minima. We derive new relationships between the minima of power bases and those of integral bases, as well as the minima of S-integers. Additionally, we derive applications of these bounds to curve theory, deriving an upper bound for the genus of a curve defined by the failure of its power basis to have a certain minima value. We also derive an upper bound for the j-invariant of an elliptic curve when its successive minima fall below a certain threshold.

This approach overcomes the limitations of picosecond ps CARS, which is limited to measuring one type of frequency. By combining a ps and femtosecond fs system, we have demonstrated the ability to perform both types of measurements simultaneously. This hybrid setup allows for the measurement of temperature, pressure, and oxygen/nitrogen concentrations in a single shot, even when the laser pulses are as short as picoseconds. The technique has been validated through numerical simulations and experimental tests, which have shown that it can accurately measure temperature, pressure, and oxygen/nitrogen concentrations in a single shot, even when the laser pulses are as short as picoseconds. The technique has also been shown to be robust to variations in the optical path length and the presence of other gases. Recent observations of protoplanetary disks have revealed the presence of warm, dense rings of gas and dust, which may be crucial in the formation of planetary systems. These features are believed to be influenced by the formation of vortices within the disks, which can trap material and accelerate the development of planets. However, the mechanisms behind vortex formation in protoplanetary disks are not yet fully understood. In this study, we investigate the characteristics of these ring-like structures and their relationship to the dynamics of the disks. By analyzing observational data from multiple protoplanetary disks, we explore the conditions under which Viscous Instability Vortices form and assess their potential role in planetary development. Our findings suggest that these structures are widespread and exhibit distinct properties, which may be indicative of their origin. We also identify key parameters that can be used to further study the formation of planetary systems.
