A new technique for detecting molecular outflows has been applied to 11 massive young stellar objects (MYSOs) in the Carina Nebula, revealing significant variations in their mass growth rates. Using the outflow-leveraged method, researchers found that the growth rates of these MYSOs are significantly higher than what was previously observed with other methods, such as ALMA-based continuum observations. The results also show that the growth rates of massive stars are not uniform, but rather fluctuate significantly over time, with some stars experiencing mass growth up to 10 times higher than their neighbors. The study also found that the mass growth of massive stars is closely linked to the presence of a companion star, with binary systems showing more frequent mass accumulation and mergers than single stars. These findings suggest that episodic mass accumulation and mergers may play a crucial role in the development of massive stars.

In this study, we examine the structure of wedge-local quantum field theories, particularly those with a finite number of particle types and massless particles, by utilizing endomorphisms defined by Longo and Witten. Our analysis enables us to determine the algebraic relationships within the net of local algebras, specifically the interplay between local algebras and those associated with the superselection sectors. Building upon the findings of Longo and Witten, we also establish the double commutant property for the net of local algebras under certain conditions.

The study focuses on quantifying the radio waves emitted from 5G cell towers in the United States, specifically examining the amount of radiation released above children, teenagers, schools, and hospitals. Utilizing data from 5G cell towers, the researchers developed a method to assess the radiation emitted in these areas. The results indicate that the majority of 5G cell towers do not emit significant radiation above children, teenagers, schools, and hospitals, with only a small percentage of towers meeting this criterion. The findings are presented through a combination of statistical analysis and visual representation.

This research paper proves a Dysthe-type formula for the Hamiltonian of water of finite depth, taking into account a constant vorticity and a uniform flow, under conditions of constant density and the presence of a free surface. We also establish a new Dysthe-type theorem for water with a constant density and a free surface, and show that the Hamiltonian can be expressed as a sum of Dysthe and Stoker components.

This paper introduces the concept of locally convex differential structures on locally convex open sets in $\mathbb{R}^n$, and proves a Stokes theorem for a specific type of integration, known as the Gelfand-Loiseraux integral, over an open set that is convex in a local sense.

This paper introduces an innovative sonar data processing framework that seamlessly integrates multiple sonar images in real-time, utilizing a vast array of sensors and navigation systems. A key feature of this framework is its ability to handle diverse sonar data formats and frequencies through an integrated data synchronization mechanism. To achieve real-time image integration, we developed an original algorithm that employs a novel method of sonar image binning, eliminating the need for a large buffer and minimizing latency. This algorithm is particularly effective in processing up to 1000 sonar images per second, making it suitable for operation on embedded systems with limited processing power. As a result, this algorithm enables pilots to make more informed decisions by providing a clear and comprehensive view of their surroundings.

This study focuses on developing a fraud detection system for online news articles, a task made challenging by the vast amount of information available and the difficulty in identifying deceptive content. To address this issue, we explored the use of automatic text summarization techniques to create a robust fraud detection model. By leveraging multiple summarization algorithms and combining their outputs with various machine learning methods, we developed a pipeline capable of accurately identifying fraudulent news. Our approach outperformed existing baselines, achieving a fraud detection accuracy of 99.99%, and we made our code and models publicly accessible to facilitate further research in this area.

This paper introduces the concept of the bending influence in high-dimensional Gaussian random fields, specifically focusing on derivatives and integral functionals. We introduce a novel decomposition for $C^2$ functionals that includes a term representing the "bending influence" and establish conditions under which this concept can be extended to Gaussian fields that are not smooth. We then prove a central limit theorem for a broad category of functions with variable smoothness, taking into account the bending influence. As a result, we obtain an Edgeworth expansion for such functions, which provides a more accurate approximation of the distribution function. This extension of previous research allows for a more accurate approximation of the tail probabilities of the Kolmogorov functional, a critical component in the study of the Brownian motion.

This research focuses on developing a secure non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) system that utilizes command decoding to decode a shared code between the base station and an untrusted eavesdropper. We examine two scenarios: one where the code is known to the adversary and another where it is not. By analyzing the achievable secrecy rates for both cases, we demonstrate that when the code is unknown, the capacity region can be attained. In contrast, when the code is known, we derive an outer bound and a corresponding achievable secrecy rate region. Furthermore, we introduce a novel technique to transform any code into an untrusted decoder, thereby enabling the application of the code's achievable rate region.

This study focuses on analyzing the IPCE problem, a variation of the principal component examination problem that uses the $\ell_1$-norm and is invariant to rotations. We investigate the local optimality of zero in IPCE problems and develop a method called Iterative Proportional Weighted Least Squares (IPWLS) to solve it. IPWLS is an extension of the well-known IRLS algorithm and is designed to converge linearly to a local optimum. The algorithm's convergence is proven under certain conditions, and its performance is demonstrated through experiments on both synthetic and real-world data. The results show that IPWLS can effectively recover underlying structures from corrupted data, even when the data is sparse and contains outliers.

Emotion-related question answering systems utilize semantic annotations to identify the sentiment expressed in questions and pinpoint the specific aspects that convey this sentiment.
These annotations are essential for training high-quality sentiment analysis models.
However, as language evolves, the accuracy of existing annotations can be compromised, necessitating their revision.
This paper presents a novel approach to revising annotations for emotion-related questions by leveraging BERT-based models.
We first employ BERT to classify the sentiment expressed in questions and then employ a combination of BERT and language generation models to generate aspect annotations.
This approach is designed to be cost-effective, as it only requires a small number of manually annotated examples to guide the revision process.
We conducted a comprehensive evaluation of our approach on two widely used datasets, showing significant improvements in annotation quality compared to existing methods.
Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical benefits of our revised annotations by training a sentiment analysis model, which outperformed models trained on existing annotations.

We examine the impact of adding order relations to the basic concepts of total functions and partial functions within the framework of Tarski's classical algebraic logic, specifically in the context of algebraic structures that are defined by their total functions and ordered structures. We then explore the consequences of this modification on algebraic structures that are defined by their partial functions and demonstrate how this change can be applied to develop a unified algebraic approach to understanding the interconnections between algebra and algebraic complexity theory.

We have analyzed 12 asynchronous polars and 10 systems with normal spin synchronization using X-ray data from the MAXI/GC and Swift/XRT missions. Our study examined the relationship between X-ray hardness and the degree of spin asynchrony. We found that the X-ray hardness of asynchronous polars does not correlate with their degree of asynchrony, which is consistent with our previous results. However, we also observed that the X-ray hardness of systems with normal spin synchronization is generally harder than that of asynchronous polars.

This study presents an innovative approach to resolving time-dependent Fluid-Structure Interaction problems by integrating two recent methodologies: a reduced basis technique and a domain decomposition strategy. By combining these approaches, we aim to tackle complex FSI problems characterized by non-matching grids and non-linear behavior. The proposed method involves partitioning the computational domain into separate fluid and structure regions, each solved using a reduced basis technique. The resulting methods are mathematically rigorous and yield optimal convergence rates for both the fluid and structure components. The algorithm's efficiency is demonstrated through numerical simulations of various problems, including a flow over a flexible cylinder and a blood flow simulation.

In unfamiliar environments, a mobile robot's navigation is complicated by the need to create a map and plan a route simultaneously. Recent studies have focused on developing simultaneous mapping and path planning methods using deep learning, but they often overlook a key aspect: the topological organization of map features. To address this, we propose HiTMap, a simultaneous mapping and path planning framework that leverages a hierarchical topological layout representation. This approach involves mapping the environment using a grid-based layout and a hierarchical graph, which captures the topological relationships between layout elements. We then employ a multi-task neural network to map sensor data to both representations and plan a route using a graph neural network. Experiments conducted in simulated and real-world settings demonstrate that HiTMap outperforms existing methods in terms of mapping accuracy and path efficiency.

This paper outlines our approach and outcomes for Task 2 of the 2018 Social AI and Language Evaluation competition, which focused on detecting aggressive language in tweets. Our team achieved a highly competitive result, ranking second overall, with a macro F1 score of 0.7384. We employed two distinct methods, utilizing a single BERT model and an ensemble of four linear Support Vector Machine models, which yielded the final ranking.

Our research proposes an innovative atomic interferometry method to measure local magnetic field changes with high sensitivity. By utilizing the Meissner effect in superconductors, we can isolate and amplify the magnetic field effects on atomic interference patterns. This method enables us to detect minute variations in local magnetic fields, such as those found in the brain, with greater accuracy than current techniques.

In this study, we theoretically investigate the spin-polarized magnetocaloric effect in monolayer MoS$_2$ using a tight-binding model, considering its proximity to a ferromagnetic insulator. Our analysis reveals that the Heisenberg exchange interaction, induced by the proximity effect, can be harnessed to achieve a significant spin-polarized magnetocaloric effect. Notably, we find that the maximum entropy change in our model is approximately 1.5 times greater than that of bulk MoS$_2$. Furthermore, we find that the maximum entropy change is achieved when the exchange interaction strength is around 0.1 times the bandwidth, and that the effect is most pronounced at the Dirac point.

Our study investigates the impact of electron spill-over and nonlocality on gap-plasmons in nanostructures with extremely small gaps. By applying a nonlocal model, we determined electron density and potential within such structures, and found that in the limit of very small gaps, the interaction between electron densities becomes negligible. We also discovered that electron spill-over significantly influences the gap-plasmon frequency, causing it to decrease as the gap size shrinks. This effect is particularly pronounced in structures with very small gaps, where the gap-plasmon frequency becomes almost independent of the gap dimensions.

We have developed a robust normalization technique for the Calculus of Constructions, which can effectively handle various proof-relevant extensions and multiple assumptions about equality, even in situations where these assumptions may be inconsistent with the calculus's core theory.

Quantum mechanics and topological mathematics have long been studied in isolation, 
yet recent breakthroughs in quantum technology have made it possible to observe 
topological phenomena within quantum systems. 
Using the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model, 
we undertook an educational exploration of the relationship between quantum mechanics 
and topological mathematics. 
By examining the SSH Hamiltonian and its associated observables, 
we discovered that certain properties, 
such as the winding number, 
can be expressed in terms of measurable quantities, 
such as the phase differences between neighboring particles. 
This connection between abstract mathematical concepts 
and physical quantities provides a deeper understanding 
of the SSH model and its associated phenomena, 
such as the emergence of zero-energy states. 
Our findings demonstrate that the SSH model serves as an ideal platform 
for studying the intersection of quantum mechanics and topological mathematics, 
and that this intersection has significant implications 
for the development of new quantum technologies.

This paper provides a novel perspective on finite mixture models through the lens of probabilistic geometry and Choquet theory. We establish the connection between the parameters of a mixture model and the geometric properties of a specific set of vectors, which can be interpreted as a weighted collection of vectors. We demonstrate that the parameters of a mixture model are equivalent to the expected values of a random variable, which is selected from a probability distribution over the given set of vectors. We further explore the implications of this equivalence, including the identification of conditions under which a given expected value can be achieved through a specific probability distribution. We also discuss the consequences of this theory for the well-known problem of identifiability in mixture models.
We develop a dual-loop supergravity theory on AdS$_5\times$S$^5$ by applying a dual-loop sigma model to the four-dimensional conformal field theory.

High-performance GPU applications require efficient memory management to optimize performance, especially when working with large amounts of data.  However, existing memory allocators for GPUs are limited in their ability to handle concurrent allocation and deallocation requests, which can lead to decreased performance.  To address this issue, we have developed a new concurrent memory allocator called DynaSOAr, which utilizes a lock-free algorithm to allocate and deallocate memory in real-time.  Our allocator is designed to minimize memory access conflicts and improve overall performance by leveraging the GPU's architecture.  We have evaluated DynaSOAr against other memory allocators and found that it outperforms them in terms of speed and efficiency, especially when working with large amounts of data.  Our results demonstrate that DynaSOAr is a significant improvement in GPU memory allocation and can help developers create high-performance applications that work with large amounts of data.

This paper investigates the boundedness of a specific class of operators, including sublinear operators and their commutators, when mapping from generalized mixed Morrey spaces to generalized mixed weak Morrey spaces. Boundedness conditions are established for these operators under certain conditions, and sufficient conditions for a class of operators are also proven.

This work utilizes a first-principles approach to investigate the electronic and magnetic properties of an Mn adatom and Mn dimers situated on the Nb(110) surface.  The study employs the initial principles of the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states in the context of the Bogoliubov--de Gennes formalism, and the results are compared to conventional density functional theory.  The analysis of the local density of states for the Mn adatom and dimers is carried out, and the spin-resolved g-factors are calculated for both cases.  The calculated spin-resolved g-factors for the Mn adatom and dimers are found to be 1.5 and 1.3, respectively, which are significantly lower than their free-space counterparts.

This paper introduces FourierMask, an innovative instance segmentation framework based on implicit neural networks. By leveraging Fourier series to map spatial coordinates into frequency domain, FourierMask enables a highly compact representation of object boundaries and masks with a significantly reduced number of parameters. Experimental results on ShapeNetPart dataset demonstrate that FourierMask achieves outstanding performance in both accuracy and efficiency, surpassing existing methods while requiring minimal training time.

This paper explores the concept of restricted, boundary-preserving, and torus-range immersions for compact surfaces, extending previous work by H. Gluck and T. Schaefer. Building on their research, we examine the immersions of a compact surface with boundary, specifically a surface with $g$ genus and $n$ boundary components. Our findings indicate that such a surface can be immersed in a way that maintains the convexity of its boundary within a torus-like region, given any value of $g$ greater than or equal to 0 and any value of $n$ greater than or equal to 1.

This study utilizes cloud images from the Multi-angle Imaging SpectroRadiometer (MISR) and MODIS to enhance our understanding of the complex internal structure of opaque convective clouds. By analyzing these multi-platform datasets, we aim to reveal the hidden spatial organization within these clouds, specifically the distribution of sunlight-reducing regions known as the "Veiled Core." Utilizing a statistical approach, we found that the veiled core typically forms in the lower half of the cloud, with its size and intensity varying based on cloud depth. Our findings suggest that the spatial distribution of the veiled core can provide valuable insights into the complex internal structure of opaque convective clouds, which can inform our understanding of cloud-radiative interactions and improve climate modeling.

A novel propulsion method, combining self-induced translucency with frequency modulation, is proposed for spacecraft traveling at high speeds. This method involves using a plasma shield to reduce drag from interstellar hydrogen, with the shield's properties adjusted to maintain translucency throughout a hydrogen cloud. By leveraging the effects of general relativity, the modulation process is simplified, allowing for more efficient fuel usage. A theoretical model demonstrates that a spacecraft with this propulsion system can achieve significant speed gains, with a 1000 kg vehicle accelerating to 0.1c in approximately 10 years. Furthermore, this method can be applied to ion propulsion, enabling the vehicle to accelerate indefinitely as it moves through a hydrogen cloud.

The K-type star TOI-712, located 100 parsecs away, hosts a planetary system with three confirmed planets and possibly a fourth. The planets, TOI-712 b, c, d, and e, are all in the early stages of development, with masses ranging from 4.5 to 10.5 Earth masses and orbital periods between 10.5 and 19.5 days. The detection of these planets was made possible by combining data from the TESS and HARPS instruments, which revealed a potential additional planet, TOI-712 e, through transit timing variations. The system's architecture, featuring a compact configuration of mini-Neptunes, is unique as it extends into the habitable zone, where a temperate super-Earth could potentially exist.

This research utilizes first-principles calculations to investigate the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen impurities in TiO2 with a rutile structure. Using a range of atomic positions and orientations, we examined the impact of p-element substitution on the material's electronic and magnetic behavior. Our findings indicate that carbon and nitrogen atoms can adopt various configurations, with some resulting in localized magnetic moments and others in non-magnetic states. Notably, nitrogen substitution can lead to the formation of a direct band gap, while carbon results in an indirect one. Our results provide valuable insights into the potential applications of carbon and nitrogen-doped TiO2 in photocatalysis and optoelectronics.

This paper introduces the concept of the "Elastic Potential," a method for identifying new phenomena in the production of top quarks that are not accounted for by strong interactions. It outlines how to detect the presence of new particles, such as Higgs bosons, in the final state of top quark pairs. The discussion also covers the use of an "Elastic Potential" in searches for the production of single top quarks and the possible implications for the study of the charge asymmetry between top and anti-top quarks.

To understand the turbulent motion within the intra-cluster medium, we need to measure velocity fluctuations within specific ranges of spatial scales. However, current methods for estimating these fluctuations are often inaccurate due to inaccuracies in accounting for measurement errors. A common approach to this problem is to apply a correction factor to the fluctuation estimates, which we find to be insufficient. We propose an alternative method that more accurately accounts for the inaccuracies in the estimation of second-order structure functions, which are commonly used to study turbulent flows. We demonstrate that this method can be applied to a commonly used dataset of X-ray observations of the Perseus cluster, which shows evidence of turbulence. We find that the estimated fluctuations in this dataset are significantly underestimated, which leads to an overestimation of the turbulent energy cascade rate by a factor of approximately 10. We also discuss the implications of this finding for other datasets that show evidence of turbulence.

In 1975, Graham and Rothschild explored the concept of infinite graph colorings, specifically focusing on the existence of monochromatic structures within infinitely colored graphs. They established that if an edge-colored graph with infinite edges is colored with a finite number of colors, there exists a monochromatic structure within a specific subgraph. In 2011, Balogh, Bollobas, and Veszeri expanded this research by investigating a related question, involving the coloring of graph components within a graph that consists of a countable number of disjoint components. They proved that if an edge-colored graph is colored with a finite number of colors, there exists a monochromatic structure within a specific subgraph. In this research, we establish a connection to a previously unexplored question and provide a proof that if an edge-colored graph is colored with a countable number of colors, a monochromatic structure is not always present within a specific subgraph.

Located at the heart of the Milky Way, the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) is a vast, anisotropically shaped region with a high concentration of gas. Understanding the mass distribution within this area is crucial for studying the dynamics of the CMZ. This study focuses on a specific part of the CMZ, known as the Central Bar Segment (CBS), where gas is observed to be highly elongated. Using a novel 2D correlation function approach, we analyze the mass configuration within the CBS, revealing a distinct anisotropic pattern. This pattern is characterized by a higher probability of gas clumps being found along the long axis of the CBS, a feature that is most pronounced at intermediate scales. This discovery suggests that the elongated mass configuration within the CBS may be influenced by the passage of gas through this area, a process that is consistent with the observed kinematic properties of the region.

This paper introduces a novel approach to identifying Bell's palsy through
analysis of facial video, specifically focusing on eye movement. A unique
methodology is employed, utilizing a detection system that identifies the
presence of Bell's palsy by detecting eye-centered symptoms. The proposed
approach is innovative in its simplicity and efficiency, requiring minimal
processing time and memory. The system's performance is validated through
testing on a diverse dataset of facial videos, demonstrating its effectiveness
in detecting Bell's palsy with a high level of accuracy. The results indicate
that the proposed approach outperforms existing methods in terms of both
accuracy and processing time. The system's simplicity and efficiency make it
an attractive option for real-world applications, such as remote diagnosis
and telemedicine. The proposed approach is a significant contribution to the
field of medical image analysis, offering a new perspective on the detection
of Bell's palsy through eye-centered detection. The results indicate that the
proposed approach is a promising solution for the detection of Bell's palsy
through analysis of facial video.

Quantum simulations of the SU(2) gauge theory in QED have been recently
achieved, and researchers are now investigating whether adding an extra degree of
freedom to introduce QCD's color charges could lead to even more groundbreaking
results. In this study, we examine an expanded version of sQED that includes
these additional charges, and we demonstrate that this larger model can be
simulated using qutrits, which are three-level quantum systems. By comparing
this larger model to its sQED counterpart, we find that the extra charges lead to
significant differences in the systems' behavior, and we observe that the
systems' dynamics become increasingly distinct as the number of charges grows.
These findings suggest that simulating this expanded version of sQED could
provide valuable insights into the complex behavior of QCD.

A new method for generating high-density polarized positrons is proposed,
involving a two-step process. Initially, a thin layer of magnetic material is
exposed to an ultra-intense laser, which causes the emission of a localized,
high-strength magnetic field. When an electron beam passes through this area,
it experiences the combined effects of the laser and magnetic fields, resulting
in the creation of numerous polarized positrons through the interaction of
photons with virtual protons. Theoretical analysis shows that this process can
produce thousands of positrons within a very short time frame, with a high level
of polarization exceeding 99%. The resulting positrons have an energy level of
around 10 MeV and a high level of density, with up to 10^12 positrons per cubic
centimeter. The process is highly efficient, with a high level of polarization
and a high level of density, making it a promising candidate for various
applications in high-energy physics.
We investigate the algebraic diameter of finite groups, specifically focusing on group varieties that have finite cohomological dimension.

This study introduces a compact and low-power temperature sensor capable of detecting minute temperature fluctuations.  The sensor employs a novel 0.6V$-$1.8V power supply range, enabling it to operate at extremely low power levels.  It features a high-resolution (0.2{\deg}C) and low-error (1.4{\deg}C) temperature conversion process that consumes minimal energy (1.06nJ per conversion).  The sensor's design utilizes a temperature-to-digital converter with a high-resolution (0.2{\deg}C) and low-error (1.4{\deg}C) temperature conversion process that consumes minimal energy (1.06nJ per conversion).  The sensor's design utilizes a temperature-to-digital converter with a high-resolution (0.2{\deg}C) and low-error (1.4{\deg}C) temperature conversion process that consumes minimal energy (1.06nJ per conversion).

The study investigates the stability of axially symmetrical magnetic fields within stars, 
considering both the effects of rotation and thermal gradients. The analysis focuses on 
axially symmetrical perturbations and employs the energy variational principle to derive 
an inequality that determines the conditions for perturbation oscillations. The study 
also derives an expression for the change in total energy under small perturbations, 
which is used to investigate the impact of magnetic field rotation on stability. The 
results indicate that the presence of magnetic field rotation can lead to the 
stabilization of certain configurations that would otherwise be unstable. The study 
further derives an expression for the frequency of small oscillations of perturbations, 
which is used to determine the conditions for perturbation stability. The study 
considers various types of stellar models, including polytropic and isothermal models, 
and derives the conditions for perturbation stability in each case. The study 
demonstrates that the presence of magnetic field rotation can lead to the 
stabilization of certain configurations that would otherwise be unstable. The study 
further derives an expression for the frequency of small oscillations of perturbations, 
which is used to determine the conditions for perturbation stability. The study 
considers various types of stellar models, including polytropic and isothermal models, 
and derives the conditions for perturbation stability in each case.

We develop a new numerical method to solve the renormalization group equations of Wilson and Polchinski in a quantitative manner. This approach is particularly useful for studying quantum field theories with a large number of components, as it can be applied to any such theory. Our method is demonstrated using a specific type of theory, known as an $N$-component scalar field theory, in $d=3$ dimensions, as it provides a clear example of the method's effectiveness. By utilizing a combination of continuous and discrete variables, we are able to solve the renormalization group equations in a tractable manner. Our results show that our method is able to accurately reproduce established results for critical exponents, as well as provide new insights into the behavior of the theory. Our method is also shown to be consistent with other established approaches, such as the epsilon expansion and Monte Carlo simulations. Our results have implications for the study of phase transitions and critical phenomena in a wide range of physical systems.

Music is a complex and captivating art form that has been the subject of extensive research, yet it remains an enigmatic world that is difficult to fully comprehend. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel approach to music analysis that combines human intuition with machine learning, allowing for a more comprehensive exploration of the intricacies of music. Our framework, Pied Piper, is designed to facilitate a variety of meta-inquiries, including the creation of customized music playlists, the discovery of similar songs, and the generation of high-quality similar tracks. By leveraging state-of-the-art machine learning models and a diverse set of music features, Pied Piper is able to provide a range of valuable insights into the music landscape, ultimately leading to more engaging and informative music recommendations.

This article explores various geometric structures on Lie groupoids and smooth stacks, including connections, curvature, torsion, and the Fefferman-Bourguignon obstruction, by leveraging the language of differential graded (DG) algebras and DG modules.

We have utilized the ALMA to examine the central 1000 AU of a massive star-forming region, the Dragon infrared dark nebula, and have discovered a dense core with an estimated radius of 400 AU. This core exhibits a mass of approximately 0.01 solar masses, a mass-to-radius ratio of around $10^{-5}$ solar masses per AU, and a temperature of approximately 10 Kelvin. The core's properties are indicative of a developing central region, and its characteristics are similar to those observed in other early-stage massive star-forming regions. The discovery of this dense core provides evidence for the formation of a central region in an infrared dark nebula, and may offer insights into the formation of massive stars.

We examine the G\"odel modal logics over a specific type of set theory called many-sorted first-order theories, and find that their algebras and relational structures can be broken down into components of simpler G\"odel logics and modal logic S4, all based on a particular type of set theory.

LiDAR technology has been widely used in various fields, including mapping, urban planning, and environmental monitoring, to collect 3D point data. This paper presents an overview of the applications of machine learning techniques in processing and analyzing these point datasets. We discuss the fundamental concepts of point data and the machine learning methods employed to extract valuable information from them. Furthermore, we highlight the potential for machine learning to unlock new insights from these datasets and provide a framework for future research and development in this area.

This paper explores how static random fields, which are invariant to time, behave when the underlying space is a sphere and the values are represented as real numbers. We specifically focus on random fields that follow a random matrix distribution, particularly the Gaussian random matrix model. We derive a method to calculate the expected value of a product of these random fields by using a recursive formula. This method is then applied to determine the average behavior of various mathematical expressions, such as the Christoffel-Darboux kernel and the determinant of a matrix, at specific points on the sphere.

The research discussed in this paper focuses on the spatial and temporal correlations between the highest-energy cosmic particles and the neutrinos detected by the ANTARES and Baikal-GVD experiments. The study utilizes data from the Pierre Auger Observatory and IceCube collaboration, covering the period from 2007 to 2015. The researchers have established the significance levels for the spatial and temporal correlations, finding a 2.7-sigma match between the locations of the highest-energy cosmic particles and neutrinos, as well as a 2.5-sigma match in their arrival times. The study also examines the relationship between the directions of the highest-energy cosmic particles and the movement of the Earth's magnetic field, finding no significant correlation. The findings are also presented in the context of previous research.

The complex behavior of foams is heavily influenced by their multi-scale texture, which can be seen in both 2D and 3D structures. This study focuses on the connection between a foam's texture and its friction, which is a key aspect of its mechanical behavior. Researchers used a combination of experimental and computational methods to analyze the friction within monodisperse soapy foams, and found that the friction is directly related to the foam's texture. They discovered that the friction is determined by the arrangement of foam bubbles, and that this relationship can be described using a specific mathematical formula. This study provides valuable insights into the behavior of foams and paves the way for further research into their mechanical properties.

This research focuses on classifying skin lesions as malignant or benign using a dataset of 101 images. To achieve this, we utilized a convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract features from the images, which were then fed into a support vector machine (SVM) for binary classification. To overcome the limitations of the dataset, we applied entropy to identify and remove outlier images that could skew the results. Our approach yielded an accuracy of 99%, demonstrating the effectiveness of combining deep learning and entropy in accurately identifying malignant and benign skin carcinomas.

A flexible finger of viscous fluid is rotating within a Hele-Shaw cell, experiencing a centrifugal force that causes it to spin. The finger's stability is influenced by the interplay between surface tension and the fluid's elasticity, which can be disrupted by a small perturbation, causing the finger to split into multiple fingers with different finger spacings. This phenomenon can be used to create patterns with varying numbers of fingers by adjusting the fluid's spin rate.

This paper introduces a novel approach to circumvent the issue of phase space volume fluctuations in Hamiltonian systems, a significant challenge for various applications of the Fermi's approximation. The proposed method involves utilizing Hamiltonian paths, which are sequences of Hamiltonians that smoothly transition from one to another. The technique is particularly effective in addressing the limitations of the approximation when used to study the thermalization process, specifically the free expansion process. The free expansion process is characterized by a sudden change in the system's potential, which leads to an increase in the system's phase space volume. The proposed method allows for a more accurate estimation of the thermalization process, which is essential for understanding the behavior of complex systems. A new class of cyclic carbon compounds, specifically ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H4CCCH), has been identified in the TMC-1 molecular cloud, with three different isomers being detected. Using a combination of high-resolution spectra and advanced radiative transfer modeling, researchers were able to distinguish between these isomers and determine their respective abundances. The findings indicate that the abundances of ethynyl cyclopentadiene are significantly lower than those of acetylene cyclopropane, with a ratio of approximately 10^-4. This discovery highlights the need for further investigation into the formation and destruction mechanisms of cyclic carbon compounds in interstellar space.

Neural machine translation models, particularly those utilizing attention mechanisms, have achieved remarkable success. However, the traditional application of attention only considers past information, excluding valuable future data. This study proposes an innovative approach called Look-forward Attention, which incorporates future data into the encoding process. Experimental results demonstrate that this method significantly outperforms the conventional one-sided attention, yielding a substantial improvement in BLEU scores.

The translational framework is a novel approach to evaluating and enhancing complex systems, which can be applied to any system characterized by a vast number of interacting components. The framework's capabilities are demonstrated through its application to the development of grid computing, a complex system that has been significantly influenced by a translational method. This paper outlines the framework, its underlying principles, and its potential to accelerate the development of other complex systems by providing a structured approach to problem-solving and system optimization.

A novel theoretical framework known as the dissipative combined dark fluid model has been proposed, based on the concept of combined dark matter and dark energy. Within this framework, a unified entity emerges that exhibits both dark matter-like and dark energy-like characteristics, while also displaying dissipative behavior. By applying a static, spherically symmetric metric and utilizing field equations, researchers have derived the necessary conditions for the model's stability and consistency. A specific instance of the model was developed and analyzed, with key parameters determined through field equations. Graphical representations of these parameters were generated to illustrate the model's behavior over time. The results indicate that the model is free from singularities and physically viable, with energy flowing outward.

Understanding how curiosity develops in learning processes is essential for improving education. Curiosity, a complex and subjective psychological trait, can be influenced by various factors and expressed differently by individuals. This study aims to explore curiosity's development during learning, using a multimodal approach to capture its subjective nature. We conducted an experiment with 12 university students who worked in groups of three on a complex task, while their interactions were recorded through eye-tracking, physiological monitoring, and self-reported measures. Our findings revealed that curiosity's development is shaped by multiple factors, including individual differences, task characteristics, and social interactions. We identified three distinct patterns of curiosity's development: steady growth, sudden jumps, and oscillating changes. This study contributes to the understanding of curiosity's development during learning and provides a framework for designing learning experiences that foster curiosity.

This paper introduces a novel class of spatial statistical models, Mat\'ern Gaussian Models on Graphs (MatGMoG), which are defined for any given connectivity structure. MatGMoG models are built upon a linear transformation of a Mat\'ern Gaussian process, creating a unique class of models that can be analyzed for their properties. We examine the behavior of MatGMoG models, including their relationship to other models, and investigate how they affect model fit and prediction accuracy. We also explore the use of MatGMoG models in a real-world scenario, analyzing data from a study on the impact of the 2011 Japan earthquake and tsunami on air quality.

The rise of large-scale ridesharing services has significantly impacted urban transportation, 
and leveraging this data can provide valuable insights into the layout of city road networks. 
This paper aims to develop a method for identifying urban road networks from ridesharing data, 
and our approach leverages a mathematical model to estimate traffic flow and identify the road network 
structure that best fits the observed data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through 
numerical experiments, and our results show that we can accurately recover the urban road network 
from synthetic data and a real-world dataset from Los Angeles.

We have investigated the impact of $J/\psi\to \gamma +$ invisible decays on neutrino and dark energy effective field theories, and found that the neutrino effective field theory is constrained to a scale of $10^{-5}$ GeV, whereas the dark energy effective field theory is constrained to a scale of $10^{-10}$ GeV, based on the latest experimental data.

Recently, variable stepsize semi-implicit semi-implicit methods (SDIMSIMs) have been introduced, and these methods have been shown to effectively handle stiff problems with changing step sizes. However, there was no prior implementation of variable stepsize SDIMSIMs until now. This research introduces the concept of V-SDIMSIMs and presents two novel approaches for developing these methods. The first approach involves modifying the coefficients of fixed stepsize methods to accommodate different step sizes, while the second approach uses a different basis for the numerical solution at each step. The two new methods, referred to as M-V-SDIMSIMs and D-V-SDIMSIMs, respectively, are analyzed for consistency and convergence. In addition, the consistency of the first approach is further explored through a specific case study. The performance of both methods is evaluated through various numerical experiments, including standard test problems and real-world applications, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of the newly introduced variable stepsize SDIMSIMs.

This research extends multivariate functional singular spectrum examination to a broader scope, encompassing data sets with variables that have undergone examination over different intervals. The examination's theoretical underpinnings are supported by a limiting theorem, accompanied by a practical demonstration utilizing both artificial and genuine data sets.

Recent studies have shown that automated evaluation systems (AES) are prone to being fooled by adversarial attacks, which can lead to incorrect assessments of malware and benign software. Although existing research has identified this vulnerability, it has primarily focused on specific attack methods and lacked a comprehensive understanding of the issue. In response, we have developed an innovative framework that explores the fundamental flaws of automated evaluation systems, which we refer to as being easily deceived and reactive. This framework enables us to identify new attacks that exploit these weaknesses, which we have applied to Android malware evaluation systems. Our research has also revealed that existing defense mechanisms against these attacks are ineffective, as they rely on the very AES being attacked. To address this issue, we have proposed an innovative approach that involves training a separate evaluation system to detect the presence of adversarial attacks. Our experiments have demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach, which has achieved a significant reduction in the success rate of these attacks.

In a one-dimensional random walk, the time it takes for the walker to revisit the starting point is known as the return time. This study focuses on the duration of staying within a specific area around the starting point, which is defined as the time it takes to exceed the maximum distance reached within a certain time frame. We investigate the behavior of this duration as the maximum distance increases, and find that it can be described by a cumulative distribution function that is unique and persists over time in a broad class of random walk step distributions.

The IShTAR facility in Italy is an innovative helicon plasma source designed for investigating plasma physics and material interactions in the context of space applications. This study aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of the plasma characteristics generated by the IShTAR helicon source, offering precise measurements of plasma parameters such as density, potential, and temperature. By employing a combination of plasma diagnostics, including Langmuir probes, microwave interferometry, and Thomson scattering, we have obtained detailed information about the plasma behavior. Our analysis reveals that the plasma generated by the IShTAR helicon source exhibits non-Maxwellian properties and exhibits significant deviations from ideal behavior. These findings have important implications for the design and operation of plasma sources used in space applications and provide a valuable reference for future research in this area.

This research paper examines a microbial biopesticide model that incorporates a suppression mechanism, utilizing a stage-specific approach to analyze its dynamics. Various equilibrium points are identified and their stability is determined, with a focus on the model's semi-global stability. A semi-global stable manifold is also explored, with an associated curve's behavior being investigated. Numerical simulations are conducted to illustrate the model's response to parameter changes and an implicit equation is derived to describe the stable manifold.

This study introduces a novel nucleus segmentation framework, which combines a nucleus identification stage with a nucleus segmentation stage. The proposed framework employs a two-stage approach, where the first stage utilizes a modified U-Net network to extract features from histopathology images and identify nuclei, while the second stage applies a convolutional network to segment individual nuclei. The proposed framework was tested on three publicly available datasets, and the results demonstrate its superior performance compared to existing methods.

This study builds on the work of certain researchers who explored how unitary group representations in a larger field can be linked to those in a smaller field through reciprocity theorems. We extend this understanding to specific types of representations for orthogonal and symplectic groups over a smaller field, including special orthogonal groups and symplectic groups, by demonstrating that a pair of closely related representations in the larger field can uniquely identify their corresponding irreducible representations. This uniqueness holds for generic and $\Theta$-generic representations, and we achieve this by utilizing a method that involves transferring representations and analyzing their distinguishing features.

This research focuses on graph theory, specifically examining the conditions under which an iterated line graph of a connected line graph and a hamiltonian route in a graph can be determined. We provide a novel proof for a previously established result, as well as a new proof for another result, utilizing the minimum cycle length of a graph. Additionally, we explore the connection between graph edge-connectivity and the presence of a hamiltonian route in its iterated line graph.

This study examines a solitary cell model of pyroptosis induced by SARS-CoV-2, which incorporates the cell's internal dynamics and the effects of the virus. The model reveals that anti-inflammatory treatments can delay cell death and increase the virus's infection rate. The findings suggest that the delay in cell death may provide more time for the immune system to respond and limit the spread of the virus.

In reinforcement learning, a key challenge is identifying and removing variables that are unrelated to the task at hand. These extraneous factors, which are not directly observable, can hinder an agent's ability to learn efficiently. This paper presents a novel approach to discovering and eliminating such unobserved variables, which are present in both the state and reward components of an MDP. We propose a method to automatically detect these irrelevant variables and develop an algorithm to do so in a setting where the variables are not directly accessible. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on both simulated and real-world robotic tasks.

This paper introduces HELMHOLTZ, a new tool for Tezos smart contracts that utilizes refinement types for enhanced type safety. By extending the Refinement Type system, HELMHOLTZ can validate complex Tezos protocols and agreements, ensuring their correctness through a contract-oriented approach. The tool's capabilities are demonstrated through the formalization of the Tezos protocol and the HART protocol, as well as a refinement monoid for combining contracts.

This study introduces a novel approach to understanding the inner workings of
graph convolutional neural networks (GCNNs) by leveraging a matched filtering
methodology. By analyzing the GCNN's filter as a function of frequency, we can
gain a deeper insight into its operation. We then introduce a frequency
domain-based optimization method to train the GCNN's filter, which can be
applied to both classification and clustering tasks. We also demonstrate that
this matched filtering approach can be used to interpret the Laplacian
frequency domain, thereby revealing the GCNN's ability to capture both
local and global graph structures. We further show that our method can be
applied to develop an optimized GCNN architecture, which outperforms existing
models in both classification and clustering tasks.

We develop a Chern-Simons-like action for a specific class of Einstein-scalar complex-Gauss-Bonnet gravity theories, which yields the full equations of motion. This action is particularly useful for studying systems with multiple hair configurations, as demonstrated in our research on rotating black holes and solitons in this context. By applying perturbative methods, we derive the mass, angular momentum, and chemical potential of black holes to first order in angular momentum, and we establish a one-parameter family of solitons that are in equilibrium with these black holes.

This study investigates the interplay between membranes and non-reversible symmetries, 
extending a prior work by Bravyi and Kitaev on the Fermion parity symmetry. 
We establish a connection between the K-theory group and the Brout-Englert- 
Higgs (BEH) mechanism, demonstrating that the BEH mechanism can be obstructed 
by a stable symmetry in certain cases. 
In the context of the BEH mechanism, the obstructions to this phenomenon 
can be interpreted as stable membranes, which in turn can be viewed as 
topological superconductors in higher dimensions.

In ultrasound elastography, estimating lateral displacement accurately is a significant challenge. This paper introduces a novel technique called Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture (VOSA) that leverages the Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture (VOSA) imaging method to enhance lateral displacement estimation. VOSA utilizes data from Virtual Origin Transmit (VOT) sequences to create high-resolution images with a large effective aperture, enabling precise lateral displacement estimation. By utilizing the high-resolution VOSA images as a reference, lateral displacement can be estimated accurately using a 1D algorithm, which is computationally efficient. A proposed method called VOSA-based Lateral Displacement Estimation (VOLA) is presented to estimate lateral displacement using VOSA images. Experimental results demonstrate that VOLA achieves high accuracy in lateral displacement estimation, with a root mean square error of 0.045 mm and a computation time of 0.045 s per frame on a 1080p ultrasound video.

We introduce the concept of "Rational Pseudocode," a novel approach to algorithm description that integrates visual demonstrations with mathematical equations and explanatory text. This approach addresses the limitations of traditional pseudocode, which often fails to provide a clear and comprehensive understanding of complex algorithms. As a result, pseudocode has become an indispensable tool in the fields of computer science and artificial intelligence, where it is used extensively to communicate algorithmic ideas. However, existing pseudocode formats suffer from several drawbacks, including difficulty in use, lack of standardization, and limited accessibility to non-experts. These limitations hinder the dissemination of cutting-edge algorithmic research and impede the reproducibility of experimental results. To overcome these challenges, we propose a standardized pseudocode format that leverages the power of HTML and JavaScript to create interactive and visually appealing algorithm demonstrations. This format is designed to be easily accessible and modifiable, enabling researchers to efficiently share their work and collaborate with others. We showcase the benefits of rational pseudocode through several case studies, including breakthrough algorithms from the recent NeurIPS 2023 Best Paper Finalists. We believe that adopting this standardized format will significantly enhance the clarity and impact of algorithmic research, ultimately advancing the fields of computer science and artificial intelligence.

This note delves into the area of Boolean algebraic combinatorics, specifically focusing on the minimum size of a subset $A$ of $n$ elements that guarantees the existence of a specific type of partially ordered set, known as the $k$-tuple union of $k$ copies of the 2-element chain union $V$-shaped poset, under a particular equivalence relation based on index shifting and element swapping. We derive an upper limit for this minimum size, denoted as $r(n,m,V)$, and establish a formula that equals $\frac{2^{n+1}-2}{\binom{2m+1}{m+1}}$ when $2m+1$ is a power of 2, and prove that this upper limit is the exact value for $r(n,m,V)$ in this scenario.

In the dynamic $k$-means problem, the parameters of data points change over time, and the goal is to update the $k$ cluster centers to minimize the total distance from each data point to its nearest cluster. This study presents an optimal dynamic algorithm that uses $O(\log^2 k)$ space and achieves a competitive ratio of $O(\log^2 k)$, which can be improved to $O(\log k)$ with a randomized approach. Additionally, the algorithm's competitive ratio is improved to $O(\log^{1.5} k)$ with a larger space usage of $O(k\log^2 k)$. The study also provides an algorithm with a competitive ratio of $O(\log^{0.75} k)$ and a deterministic algorithm with a competitive ratio of $O(\log^{0.625} k)$, both with a space usage of $O(k\log^2 k)$.

This study develops a hierarchical framework for a stochastic pursuit-evasion game involving multiple agents in a bounded, d-dimensional space, where the hierarchy is determined by the agents' abilities. The hierarchical structure allows lower-level entities to be captured by their superiors, who in turn can be pursued by their inferiors. The optimal strategy for each participant is derived using dynamic programming, and the resulting strategies are shown to be immune to deviations. The relationship between the hierarchical policy and the policy for a non-hierarchical system is explored, and a method for approximating high-dimensional systems using neural networks is presented. Numerical simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach.

A circular probability distribution is one that remains unchanged when its variables are shifted by a constant amount. In contrast, a nontransitive probability distribution is one where the relationship between events is not symmetric, for instance, the probability of event A being greater than event B may be greater than the probability of event B being greater than event A. This paper explores circular and nontransitive probability distributions, including uniform and normal distributions, and provides a method to generate such distributions.

Low-dose CT imaging has become increasingly popular in medical diagnostics, but dose-related noise can hinder image quality and affect diagnosis. This study proposes a novel approach to LDC denoising, combining AdaSwitch CycleGAN with Adversarial Attention Gate (AdaAG) and an AdaIN module. The AdaAG module selectively focuses on low-dose images, while the AdaIN module transfers knowledge from paired images. Experimental results show that AdaSwitch CycleGAN outperforms existing methods, achieving a 0.0001 improvement in SSIM and a 0.0002 improvement in PSNR compared to the best existing method.

We introduce SPACE-2, a novel dialogue comprehension pre-training framework that combines semi-supervised and contrastive learning with a tree-structured architecture. In this approach, we utilize multiple tasks to contrast dialogue representations, incorporating semi-supervised contrastive learning to leverage unlabeled data. Specifically, we employ two types of semi-supervised contrastive losses: one for cross-task and another for intra-task comparisons. For unlabeled data, we employ consistency regularization to ensure that the representations of augmented versions of the same dialogue are consistent. We pre-trained SPACE-2 on the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset and evaluated its performance on various single and multi-task benchmarks. The results demonstrate that SPACE-2 outperforms existing dialogue pre-training methods and achieves state-of-the-art results on most benchmarks with minimal additional tuning. Notably, SPACE-2 significantly improves the performance of downstream models when fine-tuned with limited labeled data.

This paper investigates the geometric configuration of an ideal fluid spacetime under the assumption of a conformal Ricci-Yamabe soliton and a conformal transformation of its Yamabe type. By analyzing this transformation, we can deduce that the metric of the ideal fluid spacetime is either conformally equivalent to a Robertson-Walker spacetime or is conformally cycloidal in nature.

When a distorted halo nucleus spins, the spins of its core and the halo can become uncoupled due to the nucleus's rotation, resulting in an energy-dependent separation between their angular momenta. This phenomenon is being investigated using a two-component shell model that treats the core and the halo as separate entities. By incorporating this model, researchers are able to explore the energy-dependent behavior of the nucleus's halo and its impact on the nucleus's resonance states. The study reveals that the halo's structure can be significantly influenced by the nucleus's rotation, resulting in the halo's energy-dependent behavior being observed in the nucleus's resonance states. The study also reveals that the halo's structure can be significantly influenced by the nucleus's rotation, resulting in the halo's energy-dependent behavior being observed in the nucleus's resonance states.

This paper introduces an advanced version of the video super-resolution model, BasicVSR, referred to as BasicVSR++, which incorporates two key enhancements over the original version. Firstly, the recurrent propagation process in BasicVSR++ is modified to employ a large kernel convolution, which effectively captures long-range temporal dependencies and significantly boosts performance. Secondly, the temporal alignment process in BasicVSR++ is improved by utilizing a large kernel convolution, which outperforms the original small kernel convolution used in BasicVSR. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed BasicVSR++ achieves superior video super-resolution results compared to the original BasicVSR.

This paper investigates the production of a Higgs boson in association with two vector bosons at a $\mu^+\mu^-$ collider, specifically the process $\mu^+\mu^-\to W^+W^+HH\mu^-\mu^-$, where the final state consists of four leptons and two bottom quarks. We focus on the sub-process $\mu^+\mu^-\to W^+W^+HH$, which is dominated by vector boson scattering. We utilize a method called Vector Boson Scattering Estimator (VS-Estimator) to efficiently simulate this process, which involves generating a set of phase space points that accurately represent the vector boson flux. We compare our results with a standard simulation using MadGraph5_aMC@NLO and find that our method is significantly more computationally efficient, achieving a speedup of up to 100 times. We also explore the impact of various sources of uncertainty on our results, including the PDF, scale, and muon polarization, and find that our method is robust and reliable. We also investigate the potential for using this process to measure the top quark Yukawa coupling, and find that our method could achieve a precision of up to 10% with a dataset of 1 ab$^{-1}$.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, sharing a single model can lead to destructive interference when tasks are unrelated. To address this issue, we propose a novel model-based MBML approach that employs task-specific modules within a single hierarchical framework. This approach allows for the sharing of latent representations while maintaining separate models for each task. We validate our method on various benchmarks, including continuous control and robotic tasks, and demonstrate its effectiveness in learning multiple tasks using a single dataset and a single network.

This paper provides a discrete approximation method for obtaining solutions to a nonlinear elliptic equation of the form $\Delta_{\phi}u+f(u)=0$, where $\Delta_{\phi}$ is a nonlinear Laplacian operator. Additionally, we derive a nonlinear heat flow that serves as a gradient flow for the functional $J$. This heat flow can be interpreted as the solution to a porous medium class equation $\partial_{t}u=\Delta_{\phi}u+f(u)$, and we prove the convergence of solutions to the nonlinear heat flow towards those of the elliptic equation as time approaches infinity. Our analysis extends to a broader setting, encompassing complete noncompact metric measure spaces with compact boundary.

This talk will present an updated version of Godel's Incompleteness Theorem that surpasses all previous iterations, including those by Tarski, Carnap, and Rosser. We will also provide a direct proof of the Incompleteness Theorem, which does not rely on the diagonal lemma, and discuss the limitations of formal axiomatic systems in capturing essential properties of natural numbers.

This paper extends the concept of capacity and conformal invariance from holomorphic functions to eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator in Clifford analysis, and proves a three-spheres theorem for such functions using capacity inequalities.

This paper introduces a novel approach to balanced sampling, called the sequential geographically balanced sampling method. Unlike traditional balanced sampling methods that require prior knowledge of the population, this method allows for the selection of a balanced sample from an unknown population in a sequential manner. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness through a simulation study and a real-world application, comparing its performance to simple random sampling and other balanced sampling methods.

Calibrating an eye-controlled camera is essential for accurate performance of robot tasks, and while traditional methods exist, they are costly and time-consuming. A new approach is proposed that utilizes machine learning to calibrate the camera from a single image, but this method's reliance on unlabelled data makes it susceptible to incorrect results. A more effective solution is proposed that combines a small set of carefully chosen images with an eye-controlled camera to improve the method's performance and reduce the need for a large dataset.

In solving inverse problems, the goal is to find a solution that explains observed data, which is often complicated by the presence of multiple solutions. To address this, we use a conditional generative adversarial network (CGAN) to generate a diverse set of candidate solutions that match the observed data. By using a regularization technique, we can encourage the CGAN to generate a wide range of solutions that are physically meaningful. Our approach is tested on a range of image reconstruction problems, including those with limited data and noise. The results show that our method can produce high-quality images that capture the underlying structure of the problem, even in the presence of noise and limited data.

This note addresses the issue of invariant surfaces in dynamical systems described by equations where the time derivative is replaced by a fractional derivative of order $\alpha$, with $0<\alpha<1$. We provide an analysis that confirms the nonexistence of such invariant surfaces.

Next-generation wireless networks will utilize terahertz (THz) frequency bands to achieve ultra-high data transfer rates, but the short reach of THz signals necessitates the development of multi-hop communication systems.  In these systems, beam training is crucial for establishing reliable connections between devices, but traditional methods that rely on a two-hop setup are limited.  In this paper, we investigate the challenges of enhancing beam training in a multi-hop THz communication system, specifically focusing on a linear multi-hop scenario.  We propose a novel approach that utilizes a deep deterministic policy gradient algorithm to optimize the beam training process, allowing for more efficient and reliable connections between devices.  Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, showing significant improvements in beam training performance compared to traditional methods.

The interstellar medium's impact on radio waves from distant radio sources can be studied using scintillometry, a technique that analyzes variations in the intensity of the signals. This method has been employed to investigate the structure of the interstellar medium along the line of sight to radio sources, particularly pulsars. A study of 110 observations of the bright pulsar B1133+16 in the direction of the Large Magellanic Cloud revealed a complex pattern of density fluctuations in the interstellar medium. The observed patterns were consistent with the superposition of two distinct turbulent structures, each with a characteristic size of approximately 100 to 200 parsecs and 10 to 20 parsecs, respectively. The outer structure was found to be aligned with the Large Magellanic Cloud, while the inner structure may be associated with the Local Group's spiral arms. The study also revealed that the density fluctuations in the interstellar medium were not uniform, with some regions exhibiting enhanced levels of turbulence. These findings provide valuable insights into the structure and dynamics of the interstellar medium in the Large Magellanic Cloud and its surrounding environment.

This paper introduces a novel end-to-end neural network architecture for synthesizing periodic and quasi-periodic audio signals, which we have named Quasi-Periodic WaveNet. Building upon WaveNet's success in generating audio signals, QuPeriodic WaveNet overcomes WaveNet's limitations in modeling periodic signals by employing a specialized dilated convolution neural network that mimics the behavior of a linear prediction filter. This allows QuPeriodic WaveNet to efficiently model signals with stable harmonic components, while also incorporating a switchable network module to handle signals with varying periodic characteristics. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, which yields high-quality quasi-periodic audio signals with low harmonic distortion and low mean squared error, outperforming the original WaveNet model.

This study introduces MADARi, a web-based platform for annotating Arabic text at a word-level, including morphological analysis and lemma identification.  The site enables users to mark up text interactively, utilizing a user-friendly interface that displays the underlying morphological structure of each word.  The platform is specifically designed for Arabic and incorporates features to facilitate the annotation process, such as a built-in morphological analyzer and a database of common Arabic words.  The code and web application for MADARi are made available on GitHub at the following URL: https://github.com/ahmed-ahmed2000/MADARi.

This study develops a photochemical model for temperate terrestrial planets,
incorporating spectral analysis to assess the impact of atmospheric composition
on observed spectra. We analyze the transmission spectra of these planets,
considering various scenarios of atmospheric presence and absence, as well as
variations in spectral analysis techniques. We find that the presence of an
atmosphere significantly alters the transmission spectra, with gas-laden planets
exhibiting broader and deeper spectral features. We also find that the
detection of molecular species such as CO2 and H2O is feasible with current
and future telescopes, such as the James Webb Space Telescope. We also find that
the spectral features of gas-laden planets can be used to distinguish between
different atmospheric compositions, with distinct spectral signatures for CO2-
rich and H2O-rich atmospheres. We also find that the spectral analysis of
gas-free planets reveals distinct features in the near-infrared spectrum, with
silicate and iron absorption bands being prominent. We conclude that the
detection of these spectral features can provide valuable insights into the
nature of exoplanet atmospheres and surfaces, with implications for the search
for habitable worlds.

In this study, we suggest using tunneling spectroscopy with linearly damped systems to differentiate the zero-bias peak caused by Majorana modes from other peaks. We derive a model for a tunneling system with linear damping and show that the Majorana peak remains prominent in the linear damping model, while other peaks are significantly suppressed. We also derive a Kramers-breaking tunneling Hamiltonian and find that the peak due to the tunneling of a single electron is significantly suppressed in a linear damping model. We propose using tunneling spectroscopy with linear damping to differentiate the Majorana peak from other peaks, and we demonstrate that the peak due to the Majorana mode is robust in a linear damping model, while the peak due to a single electron is significantly suppressed. We also show that the peak due to the Majorana mode is robust in a Kramers-breaking tunneling Hamiltonian, and we find that the peak due to the Majorana mode is significantly suppressed in a linear damping model when the tunneling electrode has a finite capacitance. We propose using tunneling spectroscopy with linear damping to differentiate the Majorana peak from other peaks, and we find that the peak due to the Majorana mode is robust in a linear damping model, while the peak due to a single electron is significantly suppressed.
